fields.title: Amy Carmichael (For Teens)
fields.description: In a Belfast street, a teenage girl carrying a poor woman’s bundle learned that respectability was stubble and love was gold. At twenty-seven Amy Carmichael sailed for India and never came home. In the villages of the far south she found that most days ended exactly as they began, until a seven-year-old girl ran away from a temple household, climbed onto her knee and said, “I have come to stay.” This teen edition tells her story straight: the converts who lost everything, the temple children and the Indian reformers who ended the practice in law, her harsh words and her hard edges, the fall that kept her in one room for twenty years, and the love the children named Amma.

qa.question: Who was Amy Carmichael?
qa.answer: An Irish missionary, born in Millisle, County Down, in 1867, who went to South India in 1895 with the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society and stayed fifty-five years without going home. After years of travelling the villages with a band of Indian women, she began in 1901 to shelter girls in danger of being dedicated to temples, and later boys too, at Dohnavur, in what became the Dohnavur Fellowship. The children called her Amma, “mother.” She died there in 1951.

qa.question: Is the book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It names her father’s early death and her lifelong pain, the converts who lost their families, the two boys who died of cholera, the dedication of small girls to temples and the exploitation that followed for many, the babies who died, and her twenty years of pain after her fall, all plainly but without graphic detail. It also names her faults: she could be severe and imperious, she wrote harshly and sometimes unfairly about Hinduism, and her parting with the young Stephen Neill was bitter.

qa.question: What did she mean by “it does not say ‘successful’”?
qa.answer: In the villages, most days ended exactly as they began. She held on to the verse “It is required in stewards that a man be found faithful,” and wrote, “Praise God, it does not say ‘successful.’” She meant that God asks his people to be faithful, not impressive, and that there is joy in simply obeying when nothing seems to happen.

qa.question: Did Amy Carmichael end the dedication of girls to temples?
qa.answer: No, and the book is careful about this. The practice was outlawed in the Madras Presidency by the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act of October 1947, after a long campaign led by Indian reformers such as Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy and Moovalur Ramamirtham. What Amy did was shelter children, one at a time, for nearly fifty years; her witness was one of many streams that fed the reform.

qa.question: How did she treat the people she lived among?
qa.answer: She wore a sari, ate Indian food, spoke Tamil, gave the children Tamil names and raised them as Indian Christians, and she would not allow caste at Dohnavur. She wrote warmly of the courtesy and intelligence of the Hindus she met, and of the grief of families who lost a child to the Christians. But she also wrote about Hinduism in harsh terms common among missionaries of her day, and the book says plainly that a Hindu reader had every reason to object. It also reports historians who argue that reform writing harmed the hereditary temple communities.

qa.question: Where do the stories come from?
qa.answer: From the full-length biography of Amy Carmichael in the Portraits of Courage series, which quotes chiefly from her own early book Things as They Are (1903) and uses the later biographies only for facts. Stories that rest on later retelling, like the blue eyes, the fur gloves, the cave and the coffee-stained skin, are marked as such. There is also a children’s edition for younger readers.

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from her story?
qa.answer: That no is also an answer to prayer; that faithfulness matters more than visible success; that you can tell the truth about hard things without despising the people involved; that one person, even one runaway child, matters to God; and that weakness and waiting are not wasted.

qa.question: Why did she never marry?
qa.answer: She chose a path that would very probably mean she never married, and in Japan, she later told a younger colleague, she went alone to a cave to pray about her fear of loneliness. She took comfort from Psalm 34, as she knew it: “none of them that trust in him shall be desolate.” She was often lonely afterwards, but she said the promise held, and she gathered a family of hundreds who called her Amma.

fields.title: Brown Eyes
fields.body_html:
“I will give thanks unto thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: Wonderful are thy works; And that my soul knoweth right well.” — Psalm 139:14 (ASV)

Amy Beatrice Carmichael was born on 16 December 1867 in Millisle, a small village on the coast of County Down, in the north of Ireland. Her father, David, ran flour mills, like the Carmichael men before him. Her mother, Catherine, was a woman of warm, steady faith. Amy was the first of seven children, and the house was full and noisy.

The family were Presbyterians, and the children learned the Shorter Catechism by heart. Its first question is “What is the chief end of man?” The answer: “Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.” Duty and delight, held together. Amy lived the first half with a seriousness some found severe. But those who knew her best remembered the second half too: her joy in God, in children, in birds and streams, and a sense of fun that never left her, even in pain.

She was a lively, strong-willed girl who loved the sea and led her brothers into adventures. She also took prayer seriously, and she expected God to answer.

The best-known story of her childhood is one she told herself, many years later. Her eyes were brown, and she wanted blue ones. Her mother had taught her that God answers prayer, so one night she asked him to change them. In the morning she ran to the mirror. Still brown. She was disappointed, but she learned something she never forgot: no is an answer too.

Be a little careful with this story. It comes from her own memory, told late in life, and the ages given for it vary, from about three to about five. People later tied it to India, where she wore Indian dress and on some journeys darkened her skin so she could go where a European would be turned away. Brown eyes could pass; blue ones couldn’t. Whether she saw that connection at the time, or others drew it afterwards, nobody can say. And not every unanswered prayer turns out to have a neat explanation. In India she would pray for children who died and friends who were not healed, and get no explanation at all. What the girl at the mirror learned was simpler: God is not a vending machine. He is free, and his refusals can be trusted.

When she was about twelve, she was sent across the sea to a Methodist boarding school in Harrogate, in Yorkshire. She was clever, but not a model pupil. Her biographers tell a story, taken from her own later memory, that in the autumn of 1882, when a great comet hung in the early morning sky, she organised a party of girls to slip out of bed to watch for it, and was very nearly sent home in disgrace. Whatever the details, it fits: the woman who would one day set the rules for hundreds started out breaking them to see a comet.

Then, in 1883, when she was fifteen (a few sources say 1882), a children’s mission came to Harrogate. Its speakers told Bible stories and spoke plainly about the love of Christ, and they treated children as people whose answer to God really mattered. Amy had known about Jesus all her life. But there, far from home, she understood that God’s love was meant for her personally, and she received it.

Some people cross that line so quietly they can’t name the day. Others, like Amy, remember the time and the place. Neither way is better. What matters is that the faith of your parents, or your church, or your friends, becomes yours.

The psalm at the top of this page was written by someone who knew God had made him on purpose, down to the details. You may wish you had different eyes, a different face or a different family. God may say no to that prayer. His no is not rejection. It can be where trusting him begins.

One thing to do this week: write down one thing about yourself you have wished God would change. Under it, write the psalm’s words: “I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” Then ask God honestly whether your faith is your own yet, or still borrowed.

study_questions.question: What did Amy learn when her eyes were still brown in the morning?
study_questions.answer: That God hears every prayer and is free to say no, and that his no can be trusted even when it comes with no explanation.

study_questions.question: Why should we be careful with the blue-eyes story?
study_questions.answer: It comes from her own memory, told late in life; the ages given for it vary, and the link with her later disguise in India may have been drawn afterwards by others.

study_questions.question: What happened to Amy at the children’s mission in Harrogate?
study_questions.answer: At fifteen she understood that the love of Christ she had always known about was meant for her personally, and she received it. Her parents’ faith became her own.

fields.title: Gold or Stubble
fields.body_html:
“But if any man buildeth on the foundation gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay, stubble; each man’s work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire itself shall prove each man’s work of what sort it is.” — 1 Corinthians 3:12-13 (ASV)

About 1883 the Carmichaels moved to Belfast, and Amy was brought home from school. The flour business was failing. Then, in 1885, her father died. Amy was seventeen, the eldest of seven, and her mother was left with a large family, a failing business and debts. Amy became, in a real sense, her mother’s partner. At about this time she also began to suffer from neuralgia, a nerve condition that brought attacks of severe pain. It would trouble her for the rest of her life.

The most famous story of her Belfast years is one she told herself, long afterwards. One dull Sunday morning, walking home from church, Amy and two of her brothers saw a poor old woman struggling along with a heavy bundle. They turned back, took her arms and carried her load. Respectable people coming out of church could see them, and Amy felt hot with embarrassment.

As they passed a fountain in the street, words came into her mind so strongly that she turned to see who had spoken: “gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble.” It was Paul, in the old Authorised Version she knew. Nobody was there. But at home Amy went to her room alone, and she said later that she settled something with God that day.

Paul is talking about what we build with our lives. Some of it lasts; some of it burns. The test is not how it looks to other people but how it stands in God’s fire. That morning Amy saw that respectability was stubble. The love that bends down to carry an old woman’s bundle was gold. She went on struggling with pride all her life, as she admitted. But she knew where the line ran.

Her biographers record a second turning point in 1886, at a convention in Glasgow. She was struggling, and the speakers didn’t help much. What reached her was a short prayer near the end, drawn from Jude, about the one who “is able to guard you from stumbling.” She went out knowing that Christ was able to keep her. She didn’t have to strain after holiness in her own strength. That was enough.

Then she noticed the shawlies. In Belfast a lady wore a hat and a servant wore a cap. A mill girl, who could afford neither, wrapped a shawl round her head. Thousands of them walked past the churches every morning to the linen mills, where they worked long hours in hot, wet, deafening rooms. Few went to church. A girl in a shawl would have felt out of place among the hats, and many congregations made sure she did.

Amy, not much older than many of them, started a Sunday class for shawlies in a hall belonging to her church. Some members were not pleased to see mill girls on their premises. The girls kept coming, because they could tell she cared about each one. The class outgrew the room, and Amy prayed for a building. She saw an advertisement for an iron hall to seat about five hundred people, at a cost of five hundred pounds. According to the account handed down, a Christian woman named Kate Mitchell heard of the need and gave the whole sum, and a mill owner gave land off the Shankill Road. They called it the Welcome. Sources disagree on whether it opened in 1887 or in January 1889. It still stands, as Welcome Evangelical Church.

God answered her prayer, though through a wealthy woman who heard about it: not asking doesn’t mean nobody knows. Amy saw that danger and tried to avoid it.

Maybe you know the feeling from that Belfast street: being seen with the wrong person, your face going hot. Paul’s question is not “What will people think?” but “Will this last?”

One thing to do this week: notice one person at school, work or church who is left out the way the shawlies were. Do one small thing to make them welcome, even if someone sees you and you feel awkward.

study_questions.question: What did the words by the fountain teach Amy?
study_questions.answer: That what we build with our lives will be tested by God’s fire. Respectability was stubble; the love that carried an old woman’s bundle was gold.

study_questions.question: Who were the shawlies, and what did Amy do for them?
study_questions.answer: Belfast mill girls too poor to wear hats, who rarely went to church. She started a Sunday class for them, and when it grew she prayed for, and was given, an iron hall called the Welcome.

study_questions.question: What did Amy take from the Glasgow meeting?
study_questions.answer: That Christ “is able to guard you from stumbling.” She didn’t have to strain after holiness in her own strength; he would keep her.

fields.title: “Go Ye”
fields.body_html:
“And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to the whole creation.” — Mark 16:15 (ASV)

In 1889 Amy and her mother moved to Manchester to help in a mission among mill workers. Amy chose to live among them, in a dirty, vermin-ridden room in Ancoats, one of the poorest districts in the city. Within months her health broke. The neuralgia got worse, and the long hours, poor food and foul air wore her out. She had given up the Welcome Hall to come, and now she couldn’t do the work.

Then an old friend stepped in. Robert Wilson was a Quaker businessman from Cumberland and one of the founders of the Keswick Convention, which taught that Christians could know a life of rest and victory by trusting Christ and giving themselves wholly to him. He was much older, and by the usual account a widower who had lost his only daughter. In 1890 he invited Amy to recover at his country house, Broughton Grange. She stayed. He treated her as a daughter, and she called him “the Dear Old Man.” She was never legally adopted, but her early books came out under the name Amy Wilson-Carmichael. Her mother agreed to the arrangement, and that was its own quiet generosity.

At Broughton Grange missionaries came and went, and Amy heard the needs of the world round the dinner table.

Then, on 13 January 1892, alone in her room, the words “Go ye” came to her with a force she couldn’t mistake. She didn’t claim to hear a voice out loud; she was suspicious of people who did. She said that a command she had heard all her life became, that evening, a command to her. You may know what that’s like: a verse you’ve read a hundred times suddenly won’t let you go.

The next day she wrote to her mother, a widow with little money, asking her blessing to go to the other side of the world, maybe for good. Her mother’s reply, which Amy kept all her life, gave her daughter to God freely and with thanksgiving. Catherine Carmichael would die in England in 1913, and Amy would not be with her. The missionary gets the stories. The parents get the empty chair.

Robert Wilson found it harder. He was old and he loved her. Some friends told Amy plainly that her duty was to stay with him, and that she was dressing up a wish for adventure as a call from God. That was not a silly argument. Jesus himself condemned people who used religious words to dodge caring for their parents. Amy was choosing between two good things, and she knew it, and she suffered over it. In the end he gave his consent, and went on writing, praying and giving for the rest of his life.

Her first thought was China. She applied to the China Inland Mission and went to its training home in London. Then she failed the medical. The doctors said her neuralgia made her unfit for inland China. The mission she admired most had shut the door.

She didn’t believe the call had been withdrawn, only that one door had closed. Another opened. The Keswick Convention agreed to send her as its first missionary, to join Barclay Buxton, an English missionary leading a band of workers in western Japan. In March 1893, aged twenty-five, with no language training and poor health, she sailed.

Years later, in Things as They Are, she explained why she kept going on the hard days. “He said ‘Go, tell,’” she wrote, “and we have come and are telling, and we meet Him as we ‘go and tell.’” She didn’t go because she felt strong. She went because she believed the one who sent her would be found on the road.

Not every call is to the other side of the world. But Jesus’ command is not “Be successful.” It is “Go, and tell.” And going nearly always costs someone else something too.

One thing to do this week: thank someone who has let you go, or made room for you to do something hard: a parent, a grandparent, a friend. Tell them what it meant. Then ask God where he might be saying “Go” to you, even somewhere small.

study_questions.question: What happened on 13 January 1892?
study_questions.answer: Alone in her room at Broughton Grange, Amy became convinced that Christ’s command “Go ye” was addressed to her personally, as a call to go overseas.

study_questions.question: Why did some friends think she should stay?
study_questions.answer: Robert Wilson was old, loved her and needed her, and they thought her duty was to care for him. Amy saw it was a choice between two good things, not between good and bad.

study_questions.question: What happened when she applied to the China Inland Mission?
study_questions.answer: She failed the medical because of her neuralgia. She believed one door had shut, not that the call was withdrawn, and the Keswick Convention sent her to Japan instead.

fields.title: False Starts
fields.body_html:
“Trust in Jehovah with all thy heart, And lean not upon thine own understanding: In all thy ways acknowledge him, And he will direct thy paths.” — Proverbs 3:5-6 (ASV)

Amy reached Japan in the spring of 1893 and joined Barclay Buxton’s band at Matsue, a castle town on a lake in the west of the main island. Christianity had been banned in Japan for more than two hundred years, and believers had been tortured and killed. The notice boards forbidding it had come down only twenty years before.

She couldn’t speak Japanese, so she depended on Japanese Christians to interpret for her, among them a young woman she called Misaki San. It was humbling, and it taught her how much the gospel in any country depends on its own people.

Her biographers tell of a visit to an old woman who was ill and seemed close to believing. Amy was wearing English clothes, including fur-lined gloves against the cold, and she noticed the woman’s eyes drifting to the gloves. The moment passed. The woman didn’t respond. Amy went home convinced that her foreign clothes had got in the way, and from then on she wore Japanese dress. Whatever the exact details, the lesson stuck. She never thought clothes could save anyone. She did think they could get in the way.

Japanese was hard. The climate set off her neuralgia, which she started calling her “Japanese head.” Many people listened politely and went away unchanged. She learned that the mission field is not the platform, and that the stories told at conventions are only part of the truth.

Then there was the cave. Many years later she told a younger colleague that she had gone alone to a cave in the hills to pray. She was in her twenties, she would very probably never marry, and she was afraid of the lonely years ahead. There, she said, God gave her a line from Psalm 34 as she knew it: “none of them that trust in him shall be desolate.” She didn’t say she was never lonely again. She often was. But she said the promise held. The story comes only from her later memory, so hold it loosely; it fits the rest of her life.

After about fifteen months, in the summer of 1894, her health broke down badly. She left, first for Shanghai and then for Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, believing she was being guided, and she didn’t consult the committee that had sent her. To some at home it looked as if she had simply walked off her post, and their criticism was not all unfair. Feeling guided by God doesn’t excuse you from talking to the people responsible for you.

In Ceylon, late in 1894, news came that Robert Wilson had had a stroke. She sailed home at once. He partly recovered, and for some months it looked as if her missionary life was over. Japan: ill. Ceylon: called home. Some of her critics must have felt proved right.

fields.title: Faithful, Not Successful
fields.body_html:
“Here, moreover, it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.” — 1 Corinthians 4:2 (ASV)

Bangalore, high on a plateau in south India, was a comfortable place for Europeans in 1895. Amy came to learn Tamil, and was soon flattened by fever.

When she recovered, something bothered her more. Many missionaries, as she saw it, lived much like other Europeans, with big houses, servants, tennis and social calls, and kept apart from the Indian people around them. She was young, and not always fair. Missionaries in that climate often broke down because they didn’t rest, and station life was the only support many had. But her unease came from a real conviction: you can’t credibly preach the gospel while living as if the world is your home. She also admitted that the gap could never be closed completely. “No matter how far you may go,” she wrote in Things as They Are, “there is always a distance you cannot cover—yards or inches it may be, but always that fatal hiatus.”

The person who changed her direction was Thomas Walker, a missionary in the Tinnevelly district at the southern tip of India, and a fine Tamil scholar. He agreed to teach her, and in 1896 she went to live and work with Walker and his wife. It became a partnership of sixteen years. Walker was demanding, hated inflated reports, and took her seriously.

Tamil, one of the world’s great classical languages, is hard for English speakers. Amy wasn’t a natural linguist, but she wanted to speak to people directly, without an interpreter. She became fluent, and came to love it.

With a small band of Indian Christian women she began travelling from village to village by bandy, a springless bullock cart. In Tamil they got a name translated as “the Starry Cluster.” Their leader was Ponnammal, a young widow who broke with the hidden life expected of widows to join them, and became Amy’s closest Indian friend. The women could go into homes where a foreigner was unwelcome and speak of their own experience of Christ. Amy believed nothing told more than that “simple witness.”

Her book is often funny. Once the bandy rolled into a flooded pool, and “the water swished in at the lower end and floated our books out quietly.” They fished them out and went on, “somewhat damp, but happy.” A little girl spotted Amy’s sun hat and ran to tell the village: “A great white man is here! Oh what an appalling spectacle!”

But the heart of the book is how hard the work was. Day after day they told the story of Jesus and saw nothing happen. People listened politely, or stared, or wandered off. Amy called one chapter “Humdrum.” “There have been times of late,” she wrote, “when I have had to hold on to one text with all my might: ‘It is required in stewards that a man be found faithful.’ Praise God, it does not say ‘successful.’”

The biggest barrier, as she saw it, was caste: the hereditary communities that gave each person a place, a trade, a family and a web of protection. Becoming a Christian usually meant losing all of it. “Caste and religion!” she wrote. “They are so mixed up that we do not know how to unmix them.” Two fair points belong here. She saw caste mostly from the outside, as bondage, and missed the belonging it also gave. And the Indian churches were not free of caste themselves, which she admitted and grieved over.

She refused to dress up the work for readers at home. “Most days in real life,” she wrote, “end exactly as they began, so far as visible results are concerned.” And yet: “There is joy in the doing of it, there is joy in just obeying.”

We live surrounded by highlight reels. Most people’s real days, Christians’ included, look more like Amy’s: ordinary, slow, apparently fruitless. God doesn’t ask you to be impressive. He asks you to be faithful.

One thing to do this week: choose one ordinary thing you do for God that never seems to show results: praying for a friend, reading your Bible, being kind to someone difficult. Keep doing it every day this week, and thank God that the text says “faithful,” not “successful.”

study_questions.question: Who was Thomas Walker?
study_questions.answer: A missionary and Tamil scholar in the Tinnevelly district who taught Amy Tamil and worked beside her for sixteen years, from 1896 until his death in 1912.

study_questions.question: What was the Starry Cluster?
study_questions.answer: The band of Indian Christian women, led by the young widow Ponnammal, who travelled with Amy from village to village telling the story of Jesus.

study_questions.question: Why did Amy thank God that the text said “faithful” and not “successful”?
study_questions.answer: Because most days in the villages ended exactly as they began. God asked her to be faithful, not to produce results, and she found joy in simply obeying.

fields.title: Was It Worth It?
fields.body_html:
“Jesus said, Verily I say unto you, There is no man that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or mother, or father, or children, or lands, for my sake, and for the gospel’s sake, but he shall receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions; and in the world to come eternal life.” — Mark 10:29-30 (ASV)

By the late 1890s a few people, mostly young, were showing real interest in the gospel.

Their families reacted fast. A clever boy of seventeen who took the gospel’s side in an argument with the village elders was suddenly married and sent off. “It is often like that,” Amy wrote. “Just at the point where the soul-poise is so delicate that the lightest touch affects it, something, someone, pushes it roughly, and it trembles a moment, then falls—on the wrong side.”

Read these stories fairly. The families were not monsters. To them, a child who became a Christian was being lost to the family, its caste and its gods, and bringing a disgrace that could make a brother’s or sister’s marriage impossible. Many acted out of love and fear. Amy knew it. She wrote of a father who “loved him dearly” and still forced himself to flog his son, and of a mother who sat with her hair undone, wailing the death-wail for a son who had gone to the Christians.

There was the law, too. A minor couldn’t leave her parents to live with others, and a missionary who sheltered one could be prosecuted. Amy agreed with the principle. “It would never do,” she wrote, “if anyone could decoy away a mere child from her parents or natural guardians.” But in villages without birth registers, a girl had to prove she was old enough to choose, and her family held the papers. “The whole burden of proof lies upon us,” Amy wrote.

One girl, whom she called Treasure, wanted to be baptised and was ready to tell a judge so. Amy had to tell her that unless her age could be proved, nobody could protect her, and that being dragged back would be worse. Treasure asked, “Would God let them take me away? Would He not take care of me?” She stayed at home and suffered for her faith there. Amy left her readers with the question.

Some did come out, old enough to choose or with their families’ reluctant consent. One was Arulai, a girl from a Hindu family who would grow into one of the pillars of Dohnavur. Amy called converts “a responsible joy,” and she meant both words.

Then there were two boys. The younger was an only son, heir to property. His father flogged him twice. When he left home, his relatives sat round him and offered him a house, land, his inheritance at once and a rich bride, if only he would come back and save his caste. “I will not go back,” he said. A year or so later both boys were baptised together during a holiday by the sea. A few weeks after that, both died of cholera. The younger died with Hindu neighbours taunting him that this was his reward for breaking caste. Too weak to say much, he pointed upward and tried to sing.

“Was it worth the pain it cost?” Amy asked. “Such a short time to witness, was it worth while?” She had no neat answer. She noted that each boy had found one other boy, and she believed that if you could ask them, “they would tell you Jesus’ welcome made it far more than worth while.”

She also learned that publicity could be dangerous. Supporters wanted names and photographs, but a convert whose story was printed could be traced. She wrote that “we have learned by experience to fear any attempt to photograph spiritual fruit.” So she changed names in her books.

Jesus’ promise at the top of this page is generous: a hundredfold. But look at the two words in the middle: “with persecutions.” For many believers today, it still costs family, home and safety.

One thing to do this week: find out about one country where becoming a Christian is dangerous today, and pray for believers there. Then ask yourself honestly: is there anything you would find it hard to give up for Jesus?

study_questions.question: Why did Hindu families try so hard to stop their children becoming Christians?
study_questions.answer: Because conversion meant losing caste, which brought disgrace on the whole family and could ruin brothers’ and sisters’ marriages. Many acted out of love and fear, not just hostility.

study_questions.question: Why couldn’t Amy protect Treasure?
study_questions.answer: The law said a minor must stay with her family, and without birth registers Treasure couldn’t prove she was old enough to choose. Coming and being sent back would have been worse.

study_questions.question: How did Amy answer her own question, “Was it worth the pain it cost?”
study_questions.answer: Not with an argument but with faith: each boy had found one other boy, and she believed they would say Jesus’ welcome made it “far more than worth while.”

fields.title: Pearl-Eyes
fields.body_html:
“Thou hast seen it; for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite it with thy hand: The helpless committeth himself unto thee; Thou hast been the helper of the fatherless.” — Psalm 10:14 (ASV)

On an evening in early March 1901, a little girl was found alone outside the church at Pannaivilai, where Amy was living with the Walkers. She was about seven, with tumbled hair and frightened eyes, and she didn’t belong to the village. A Christian woman took her home for the night. In the morning the child insisted on seeing a particular foreign lady, and the woman brought her to the mission bungalow. The usual date given is 7 March 1901.

Amy was reading on the verandah. The child ran straight to her, climbed onto her knee without the least fear, and began to talk. “I have come to stay,” she said.

Later books call her Preena. In Things as They Are, the earliest account, written within a year or two, Amy called her Pearl-eyes, to protect her.

As a baby, the child had been given by her mother to women attached to a temple in a nearby town, whom Amy called the Servants of the gods. Nobody loved her there. Some months before, the woman who kept her had burned her little fingers as a punishment “for some childish fault.” She ran away to her mother, three days’ journey and about twenty miles off, and searched the streets until she found her. “My mother cried,” she told Amy. But the temple woman followed, and her mother gave her up again.

Back in the temple house, she overheard that she would soon be “married to the god,” the ceremony by which a girl was dedicated to a temple for life. She didn’t understand all it meant, but she understood enough to be terrified. She ran into the temple, stood before the image and prayed, “Let me die! Oh, let me die!” “Barely seven years old,” Amy wrote.

To frighten her, the temple women had pointed out one of the women of Amy’s band, passing through their town, as “the child-stealing Ammal.” It was meant as a warning. It worked the other way. The child went looking for her.

Within hours the temple women arrived. “We are Servants of the gods,” one said. She refused to go, and the missionaries would not force her. A larger crowd came later, and one woman, who clearly terrified her, demanded that she say before them all that she wouldn’t go back. The child froze. Amy dared not go near her, in case she was accused of bewitching her. Taken out of the room for a moment by Star, one of the convert girls, the child sobbed and showed the marks of earlier punishments. Then she walked back in and cried, “I won’t! I won’t!”

It wasn’t over. Under the law, the child belonged to her mother, so keeping her could count as taking a minor from her guardians, a crime. Dedicating a girl to a temple for that kind of life was already against the law in principle, but proof was almost impossible. “Only the great difficulty might be to prove it,” Amy wrote. One woman accused the child of theft; the sum turned out to be fourpence halfpenny, and the missionaries paid it. Amy and the Walkers decided to keep her and take the consequences.

Weeks later, Amy was teaching her that we are redeemed “not with corruptible things, as silver and gold.” The child broke in: “Oh yes, I understand! I know how much you paid for me—fourpence halfpenny!”

Amy saw God’s hand in the timing: a few weeks earlier the missionaries had been away, and nobody could have protected her. She called these “touches that tell how God cares.” Before this she had seen temple children and felt powerless: “no hand of ours can stretch over the wall and lift even one child out.” Now a child had climbed over the wall by herself. Everything Amy is remembered for began here, with one.

One thing to do this week: find out about one organisation that protects children at risk, near you or abroad. Pray for it by name, and ask what one small thing you could do to help, even if it’s only learning more.

study_questions.answer: She was unloved, had been punished cruelly, and had overheard that she was soon to be “married to the god,” dedicated to the temple for life.

study_questions.answer: The temple women, trying to frighten her, had pointed out a woman of Amy’s band as “the child-stealing Ammal.” Instead of scaring her, it told her where to go.

fields.body_html:
“but we have renounced the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by the manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.” — 2 Corinthians 4:2 (ASV)

Later in 1901 the household settled at Dohnavur, a village on the plain at the foot of the Western Ghats mountains. It had been founded in the 1820s as a refuge for Christians driven out of their own villages. Amy loved it at once; the mountains reminded her of the Lake District.

Other children began to arrive after Preena, and Amy found she couldn’t travel the villages and care for small children at the same time. Some fellow missionaries thought she was wasting her gifts, giving up being a missionary to become a nursemaid. But she came to believe that caring for children for Christ’s sake was as spiritual as preaching. She let her own plan go.

Two visiting friends urged her to turn her letters into a book, and offered to do the editing. Things as They Are came out in April 1903.

“The book is a battle-book,” she wrote, “written from a battle-field where the fighting is not pretty play but stern reality.” Under the village stories, it argued what readers at home didn’t want to hear: that the work was slow and hard, that most people didn’t want the gospel, that those who did often lost everything, and that cheerful missionary reports were misleading. “Do not, we entreat you, expect to hear of us doing great things, as an everyday matter of course,” she wrote.

It also named what most missionary books left out, including the dedication of girls to temples, though without lurid detail. She knew people would call the book too harrowing, and answered them in its pages: “We are told to modify things, not to write too vividly, never to harrow sensitive hearts. She believed people wouldn’t pray properly unless they knew what they were praying about.

Eugene Stock, a respected leader of the Church Missionary Society, wrote the preface: “What she says is the truth, and nothing but the truth; but it is not the whole truth—that she could not tell. If she wrote it, it could not be printed. If it were printed, it could not be read.”

Most Hindus had nothing to do with those abuses and would have condemned them, and Hindu reformers were fighting the same evils in the name of a purer Hinduism. A devout Hindu reader had every reason to object. Amy could also write with real warmth about the intelligence, courtesy and humour of the Hindus she met. Both things are true.

Paul refused to handle God’s word “deceitfully.” Amy refused to sell the mission with pleasant fictions. But telling the truth well means telling it fairly about others too.

One thing to do this week: next time you talk about your faith or your church, don’t polish it; be honest about the hard parts. And if you describe someone else’s religion, do it in a way a person who believes it would recognise as fair.

fields.title: Servants of the Gods
fields.body_html:
“Deliver them that are carried away unto death, And those that are ready to be slain see that thou hold back. If thou sayest, Behold, we knew not this; Doth not he that weigheth the hearts consider it? And he that keepeth thy soul, doth not he know it? And shall not he render to every man according to his work?” — Proverbs 24:11-12 (ASV)

This is the hardest part of Amy’s story, and it can be told badly in two opposite ways. One is a lurid tale of a brave missionary rescuing innocent girls from wicked priests. The other is a tale of a prejudiced foreigner slandering an ancient tradition. Neither is true.

For centuries some temples in India, especially in the south, had women dedicated to the service of the god. In English they came to be called devadasis, from a Sanskrit word meaning “servant of god.” A girl was dedicated in a ceremony spoken of as a marriage to the god, and after it she could never marry a man. The tradition had a long and in some ways honoured history. Some owned property and were educated when most women were not, and they kept classical dance and music alive. The dance now known around the world as Bharatanatyam comes in large part from their art.

But by the nineteenth century, in many places, the tradition had changed. Girls were dedicated in childhood: given by parents who had made a vow or couldn’t support them, bought from poor families, or adopted by older temple women. Many were drawn, as they grew up, into a life of sexual exploitation. The girl had no say. By the time she understood, her life had been decided for her.

Amy met this through children. She once talked with a learned grandmother who could recite page after page of Tamil classics. “Consider the age of our great Religion, consider its literature—millions of stanzas!” the old woman said. Her little granddaughter joined in, chanting stanza after stanza, then ran off laughing to play. Later Amy saw two men leading that same child away to be married to the god. “All that brightness, all that intelligence,” she wrote. Notice what it shows: a family of real culture and learning. Amy didn’t think the people around her were savages; she thought something terrible was being done inside a refined world.

After Preena came, Amy began asking how many girls were involved and what happened to them. (Popular stories say she went in disguise, her skin stained with coffee; the details have been embroidered.) She never published what she learned.

The campaign that finally ended the practice was led by Indians. Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy, the first woman in the Madras Legislative Council, brought forward a bill against it in the late 1920s. Moovalur Ramamirtham, from a devadasi family herself, campaigned for decades for her community’s women to be free to marry. In October 1947 the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act was passed. Amy lived to see it. It was not her law, and it should be remembered as theirs.

Fairness asks one more thing. Not everyone in those communities welcomed the reform. Hereditary temple artists protested that they were being slandered for the sins of some, and that their art and livelihood were being destroyed. Historians such as Davesh Soneji have argued that reform writing, missionary and Indian alike, including Amy’s, fixed a picture of these women as nothing but victims, and did lasting harm to their descendants. You may not agree with all of that; the children Amy sheltered were small girls who never chose. But the women of those communities were people with their own voices and dignity, not just a problem to be solved.

The proverb at the top of this page takes away our excuse: “If thou sayest, Behold, we knew not this.” Once Amy knew, she couldn’t unknow it. She didn’t lead a campaign. She took in children, one at a time. Children are still exploited today. Once you know, you’re responsible too, and you can oppose an evil without despising the people around it.

One thing to do this week: if you ever think a child, or someone your own age, is being exploited or is unsafe, tell a trusted adult or a helpline where you live. That isn’t gossip; it’s what Proverbs asks.

fields.title: The Elf
fields.body_html:
“He will feed his flock like a shepherd, he will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and will gently lead those that have their young.” — Isaiah 40:11 (ASV)

Before there were nurseries at Dohnavur, there was one small girl who wouldn’t keep still. Amy nicknamed Pearl-eyes “the Elf” and wrote a whole chapter about her. It is the happiest chapter in Things as They Are.

The Elf hated her ten minutes of polishing the brass water-pots, until she made a discovery: “Satan doesn’t come very close to me if I sing all the time I’m rubbing the brasses. He runs away when he hears me sing, so I sing very loud, and that keeps him away. Satan doesn’t like hymns.” Every evening she said her prayers in Amy’s room, counting her sins on one hand and her blessings on the other. She had been cross with another girl, she confessed, but the other girl had been wrong too, “so it was only half a sin.”

The Elf and two other small girls argued theology with real energy. Orpah obeyed Naomi and went home, they decided, while Ruth was told to go and refused; yet God blessed Ruth more, because she loved. “So obedience is not so important as love.” Amy had spent the day before trying to teach them obedience. She wrote it down anyway, laughing at herself.

The Elf also asked a question that wasn’t childish at all. She had prayed to be good, and within an hour she had been naughty. “How was it I was naughty when I wanted to be good?” she asked. “So what is the use of praying?” It is Paul’s question in Romans 7. Amy didn’t pretend it was easy.

To Amy, the children were never cases or trophies. They were people, with their own wills, jokes and sins.

From about 1904 babies began to come, because the time to protect a girl was often before she could walk. Some were brought by mothers who couldn’t keep them and would rather they went to the Christians than to a temple. Babies needed wet nurses and constant care, and many of the early ones died. Amy grieved over every one. Simple nurseries were built, each with a group of small children and the women who cared for them. In 1909 she published Lotus Buds, about these children: the lotus grows up out of mud into a beautiful flower.

The children called her Amma, Tamil for “mother.” She wore a sari, and the household ate Indian food and spoke Tamil. Each child got a Tamil name chosen with care, often as a prayer for her life. Many mission orphanages of the time gave children English names and clothes, and they grew up strangers in their own country. Amy wanted Indian Christians, not Westernised Indians.

One custom she refused: caste. Children from high and low communities ate, played and slept together as sisters. To families outside, that was one of the most offensive things about Dohnavur, because a child who went there could never go back into her caste. Amy didn’t flinch. In Christ, she believed, there is neither high caste nor low.

Most of the daily care was done by Indian Christian women called accals, from the Tamil for “elder sister”: converts like Arulai, widows like Ponnammal, and later girls who had grown up there themselves.

Amy was also strict. She expected obedience and could be severe, and some adult workers found her exacting, a few overbearing. She didn’t always tell the difference between disagreeing with her and being disloyal to the work. Those were real faults. But by most accounts Dohnavur was a happy place. She laughed easily, invented games, wrote songs, and taught the children to love birds, butterflies and streams. By 1913 there were about a hundred and thirty children.

Isaiah pictures God as a shepherd strong enough to carry the lambs and gentle enough not to drive the mothers too hard. Amy had plenty of strength. Gentleness she kept learning.

One thing to do this week: spend real time with a younger child, a sibling, cousin or neighbour, and actually listen to their questions about God. You might learn something, the way Amy learned from the Elf.

study_questions.question: What did the Elf and her friends decide about Ruth and Orpah?
study_questions.answer: That Orpah obeyed and went home, but Ruth refused to go because she loved Naomi, and God blessed Ruth more, “so obedience is not so important as love.”

study_questions.question: How was Dohnavur different from many mission orphanages?
study_questions.answer: The children kept Tamil names, Indian dress, Indian food and the Tamil language, so they grew up as Indian Christians rather than strangers in their own country. And caste was not allowed.

study_questions.question: What were Amy’s faults as the head of the household?
study_questions.answer: She could be severe and exacting, and she didn’t always tell the difference between disagreeing with her and being disloyal to the work.

fields.title: Understand Hereafter
fields.body_html:
“Jesus answered and said unto him, What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt understand hereafter.” — John 13:7 (ASV)

Robert Wilson, the Dear Old Man, died in 1905. Amy hadn’t seen him since she sailed ten years before. That was the kind of grief missionaries far from home learned to expect. The years from 1912 to 1915 were different. One after another, they took the people Amy leaned on most.

In August 1912 Thomas Walker fell ill on a journey and died, far from Dohnavur. He had taught her Tamil, stood beside her when Preena came and helped her build the household, and his steady judgement had balanced her intensity. Now everything rested on her. Soon afterwards, while they were still mourning, a lawyer wrote demanding that a wall being built round part of the compound stop at once, claiming the land wasn’t the mission’s.

On 14 July 1913 her mother died in England. Amy had not seen her since 1895. Her mother’s letter of 1892, giving her daughter freely to God, had been one of the treasures of her life. Amy was forty-five, and an orphan herself.

Her biographers record that about 1914 a kidnapping charge was brought over a girl named Muttammal whom the household was protecting, and that Amy faced possible arrest before the case was dropped. Those details can’t be checked against court records, so hold them loosely. The general picture is clear: sheltering children at Dohnavur meant living under the shadow of the courts. In August 1914 war broke out in Europe, prices rose and letters from home slowed. The household told its needs to God and not to people, and later said it had never lacked what it needed, while Amy took care not to suggest that Christians who did go without were less faithful.

The hardest loss was Ponnammal, her closest Indian friend, who had led the band and become a pillar of Dohnavur. She had a long, painful illness, described as cancer. Amy prayed for her healing, and it didn’t come. Watching her suffer without being able to help was, for Amy, harder than the death itself. Ponnammal died in 1915, and Amy took her daughter into her own care.

Amy didn’t pretend to understand. She later warned against handing easy explanations to people in pain. What she chose was acceptance: not a dull giving-up, but a deliberate decision to take from God’s hand what she couldn’t understand, and go on.

All through those same years she was praying about something else. She had learned that boys too were sometimes given to temples, or to the travelling drama companies connected with temple festivals, and that some were exploited as badly as the girls. According to the Fellowship’s own history, the burden came to her about 1912. Taking in boys would need men, buildings and money, so she prayed that God would either take the burden away or show her what to do.

For six years nothing happened. Amy was impatient by nature; when she saw a need, she wanted to meet it. Now she waited.

In January 1918 a baby boy was brought to Dohnavur. Nobody had gone looking for him. Amy took him as the answer, and the boys’ work began. In time men came to care for the boys: Indian Christians, young men who had grown up at Dohnavur, and some from Britain, among them the brothers Godfrey and Murray Webb-Peploe. Amy wanted the boys to be strong and brave, and able to earn their own living in India rather than depend on a mission.

Jesus said to Peter, as he knelt to wash his feet, “What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt understand hereafter.” It is a promise of understanding later, not now. Amy got some of the “hereafter” in her lifetime, like the boy in 1918. Some of it she never got.

If you are waiting on God for something, or grieving something you don’t understand, you are not failing at faith. That’s where faith lives.

One thing to do this week: write down one thing you have been praying about for a long time. Next to it, write Jesus’ words: “thou shalt understand hereafter.” If you are grieving, tell one person you trust how you really feel.

study_questions.answer: Thomas Walker in 1912, her mother in 1913 and Ponnammal in 1915, besides facing a legal dispute over a wall and, according to her biographers, a kidnapping charge.

study_questions.answer: Not giving up, but deliberately receiving from God’s hand what she couldn’t understand, and going on trusting him.

study_questions.answer: About six years, from around 1912. In January 1918 a baby boy was brought to Dohnavur without anyone looking for him, and she took it as God’s answer.

Taking in boys would need men, buildings and money, so she prayed that God would either take the burden away or show her what to do. For six years nothing happened. Amy was impatient by nature; when she saw a need, she wanted to meet it. Now she waited. In January 1918 a baby boy was brought to Dohnavur. Nobody had gone looking for him. Amy took him as the answer, and the boys’ work began. In time men came to care for the boys: Indian Christians, young men who had grown up at Dohnavur, and some from Britain, among them the brothers Godfrey and Murray Webb-Peploe. Amy wanted the boys to be strong and brave, and able to earn their own living in India rather than depend on a mission. Jesus said to Peter, as he knelt to wash his feet, “What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt understand hereafter.” It is a promise of understanding later, not now. Amy got some of the “hereafter” in her lifetime, like the boy in 1918. Some of it she never got. If you are waiting on God for something, or grieving something you don’t understand, you are not failing at faith. That’s where faith lives. One thing to do this week: write down one thing you have been praying about for a long time. Next to it, write Jesus’ words: “thou shalt understand hereafter.” If you are grieving, tell one person you trust how you really feel.

fields.title: Lording It
fields.body_html:
“neither as lording it over the charge allotted to you, but making yourselves ensamples to the flock.” — 1 Peter 5:3 (ASV)

In March 1916 Amy gathered a small group of the Indian women who worked with her into the Sisters of the Common Life. There were no lifelong vows, but they committed themselves to simplicity, prayer and service, and to staying unmarried for as long as they felt called, so they could give themselves to the children. In a society where almost every woman married, it offered single women a recognised life with dignity and purpose. Some people were uneasy. Amy said plainly that singleness was not better than marriage, and the girls raised at Dohnavur were free to marry. Many did.

In 1925 the link with the Zenana Society ended by agreement, and in 1927 the work was registered as the Dohnavur Fellowship. Its members received no salaries, and it made no appeals for money. Independence let Amy lead as she believed God was leading her. It also meant nobody outside could question her decisions.

That matters for what happened with Stephen Neill. He was a brilliant young fellow of a Cambridge college who came to Dohnavur in 1924, having read Amy’s books and hoping to work under her. It went badly. They seem to have disagreed over how the boys should be brought up, including how far they should be allowed outside the compound, and Neill did not easily accept her authority. Amy seems to have felt he was undermining the work and the unity of the Fellowship. In November 1925 he left. A historian who has studied the episode, Dyron Daughrity, calls it a bitter parting. Neill later wrote critically of his time there. Amy’s own history of the Fellowship doesn’t mention him at all.

Neill went on to become bishop of Tinnevelly, the very diocese Dohnavur lay in, and one of the best-known historians of Christian missions in the world. It’s worth being fair to both. He was young, gifted and sure of himself, and may have been hard to manage. She was a strong leader who didn’t easily share authority and couldn’t always tell disagreement from disloyalty. Wiser handling on both sides might have kept him. Her silence suggests the wound went deep.

Some observers said something similar about Dohnavur’s walls. In the early years, guarding the children was plainly necessary, because people who saw them as property might try to take them back. Later, some wondered whether the walls, real and invisible, had stayed higher than they needed to be, and some of the children who grew up there found it hard to make their way in the world outside. What some saw as love, others saw as control.

That isn’t the whole story. In these same years doctors and nurses joined the Fellowship, and by the end of the 1920s it had its own hospital, which Amy named in Tamil the Place of Heavenly Healing. It served the villages round about, Hindu and Christian alike. She wanted patients to see Christ’s love in their care, but nobody was to be pressured, and treatment never depended on being willing to listen. And she kept writing, including Mimosa (1924), about a girl who spent only a short time at Dohnavur, heard there that God loved her, and held on to that one truth at home for years with almost no other teaching.

Amy wanted the Fellowship to be “of one heart and soul,” like the first church in Acts. It was a good aim, and it produced a community of rare devotion. The danger is that unity slides into everyone agreeing with the leader, and the leader’s will gets mistaken for God’s. Amy warned against that. She didn’t always escape it.

Peter tells leaders not to lord it over people but to be examples. That’s hard for strong people, and if you’re a natural leader, it’s written for you. Being sure you’re right is not the same as being right, and someone who disagrees with you is not automatically disloyal.

One thing to do this week: think of someone who disagreed with you recently, in a group project, a team, a family argument or at church. Ask them to explain their view again, and listen without defending yourself. If you were wrong, say so.

study_questions.question: Who were the Sisters of the Common Life?
study_questions.answer: Indian women at Dohnavur who, from 1916, committed themselves to simplicity, prayer and service, and to staying unmarried for as long as they felt called, so they could care for the children.

study_questions.question: Why did Stephen Neill leave Dohnavur?
study_questions.answer: He and Amy seem to have clashed over how the boys should be brought up and over her authority. Both had faults, and the parting in 1925 was bitter.

study_questions.question: What is the danger in a community that prizes unity, as Dohnavur did?
study_questions.answer: That unity turns into uniformity, and the leader’s will is mistaken for God’s will, so people who disagree aren’t heard.

fields.title: Amma
fields.body_html:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it abideth by itself alone; but if it die, it beareth much fruit.” — John 12:24 (ASV)

In the autumn of 1931, her biographers record, Amy prayed, as she often had, that God would do whatever would best fit her for his service. On 24 October 1931, at dusk, she went to look at a building being prepared for the work, at Kalakadu according to her biographers. Workmen had dug a pit in the floor and left it uncovered. In the half-dark she stepped into it and fell. She broke her leg, dislocated her ankle and injured her spine. She was sixty-three.

Everyone expected her back on her feet within weeks. She never was. For almost twenty years she lived mostly in one room, often in pain, able to walk only a little. Outside her window was a bird-bath, and she watched the birds.

Was the fall God’s answer to her prayer? Amy came to believe that God had allowed it and would use it. She didn’t believe he pushed her into the pit, or that pain was good in itself, and in her better moments she didn’t pretend to understand. People all over the world prayed for her healing, and the answer was no. The girl at the mirror in Millisle learned the same lesson again, at far greater cost.

The hardest part may have been losing control. Others, Indian and British, had to take on more of the leading. That was good for a Fellowship that would one day live without her, but she found it hard to let go.

Yet out of that room came the books most of the world knows her by, among them Gold Cord (1932), her history of the Fellowship; Rose from Brier (1933), written for people in pain by someone in pain; and If (1938), a small book that measures everyday failures of love against the love of Calvary. She wrote notes, often daily, to members of the Fellowship, and letters to strangers. People noticed a gentleness that had not always been so clear in her active years.

The losses went on. Arulai, by then one of the Fellowship’s leaders, died in 1939. In August 1947 India became independent, and in October the Madras Act against temple dedication was passed. Amy stayed. The Fellowship had long been preparing for Indian leadership.

Amy Carmichael died at Dohnavur on 18 January 1951, aged eighty-three, after fifty-five years in India without once going home. She didn’t want a monument. She was buried in the Fellowship’s burial ground, called God’s Garden, among the children and workers who had gone before her. Over her grave they put a bird-bath, and on it one word: Amma.

How should her life be weighed? Honestly. Hundreds of children, perhaps more than a thousand over the years, grew up at Dohnavur who might otherwise have faced exploitation, neglect or early death, and they were given a home, a family and a faith. The Fellowship still works in Tamil Nadu today, under Indian leadership. But her writing about Hinduism was often harsh and sometimes unfair, and it did harm. She could be imperious, as the parting with Stephen Neill shows, and Dohnavur’s walls may have stayed high too long. She was a woman of her time and her empire. The shadows are real. They don’t cancel the light.

A saying often attributed to her, though rarely with a source, is that missionary life is simply a chance to die. It echoes Jesus’ words at the top of this page. She let go of Belfast and the Welcome Hall, of Robert Wilson, of the village work she loved, of her mother, of her health and finally of control. Each time something died. Each time, she believed, something grew.

And it all began with one child who walked through the dark to find her. You will probably never run a Fellowship. But you can be faithful to the one person God puts in front of you.

One thing to do this week: ask yourself what one word you would want written over your life. Then ask God whether there is something you are holding on to tightly that he is asking you to let go of, and take one small step toward letting it go.

study_questions.question: What happened to Amy on 24 October 1931?
study_questions.answer: She fell into an uncovered pit in a building being prepared for the work, breaking her leg, dislocating her ankle and injuring her spine. She was largely confined to one room for the rest of her life.

study_questions.question: What good came out of her twenty years in one room?
study_questions.answer: Many of her best-known books, a daily ministry of notes and letters, a deeper gentleness, and a Fellowship that learned to lead itself.

study_questions.question: Why does her grave say only “Amma”?
study_questions.answer: Because the name that mattered most to her, and to the children, was the one they gave her: mother. She didn’t want a monument.
